class/LayerCollector.d:
LayerCollector is the base class of 2D UI containers which render GuiObject descendants, such as ScreenGui.

For performance improvements, the appearance of a LayerCollector is cached until one of the following events occurs:

  • A descendant is added to or removed from it.
  • A property of a descendant changes.
  • A property of the LayerCollector itself changes.
class/LayerCollector.s: The base class of 2D UI containers which render `Class.GuiObject|GuiObjects` in layers.

m.d: Toggles the visibility of this LayerCollector. When false, the UI contents will not render, process user input, or update in response to changes.
m.s: Toggles the visibility of this `Class.LayerCollector`.

kid.simple: Shows (true) or hides (false) the whole UI canvas and everything inside it. When false, nothing inside is drawn, clicked, or updated.
kid.example:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local shop = playerGui:WaitForChild("ShopGui")
shop.Enabled = true -- open the shop

m.d:
When set to false and this LayerCollector is a direct child of StarterGui, it will only be cloned into each player's PlayerGui once and it will not be deleted when the player's character respawns.

When set to true (default), or if this LayerCollector is an indirect descendant of StarterGui, it will be cloned into each player's PlayerGui when their character respawns, and it will delete itself when the player's character respawns again.
m.s: Determines if the `Class.LayerCollector` resets (deletes itself and re-clones into the player's `Class.PlayerGui`) every time the player's character respawns.

kid.simple: When true (default), the UI is deleted and copied fresh from StarterGui every time the player's character respawns. Set false (and keep it directly in StarterGui) to copy it only once and keep it forever.
kid.example:
local gui = script.Parent -- a ScreenGui directly inside StarterGui
gui.ResetOnSpawn = false
kid.gotcha: A LocalScript inside a resetting Gui also restarts on every respawn.

m.d:
Controls how GuiObject.ZIndex behaves on all descendants of this LayerCollector.

With ZIndexBehavior.Sibling (default), children always render above their parents, and the ZIndex is used to decide the order in which children of a single UI object will render over each other.

ZIndexBehavior.Global sorts all descendants according to the ZIndex, then breaks ties using the hierarchy order. As a result, descendants of a GuiObject need to have a ZIndex value that's at least as high as the parent, or they will render underneath their parent.
m.s: Controls how `Class.GuiObject.ZIndex` behaves on all descendants of this `Class.LayerCollector`.

kid.simple: Decides how ZIndex works for everything inside. Sibling (default): children are always drawn on top of their parent, and ZIndex only sorts brothers and sisters. Global: everything is sorted by ZIndex together, so a child needs a ZIndex at least as high as its parent or it hides behind it.
kid.example:
local gui = script.Parent -- a ScreenGui
gui.ZIndexBehavior = Enum.ZIndexBehavior.Sibling -- the easy, default way

m.dep: This method should not be used for new work.

kid.simple: Old — use nothing (this is an internal function you don't need) instead.

LayerCollector is the family name for the 'canvases' that hold UI: ScreenGui (on your screen), BillboardGui (floating in the world, facing you) and SurfaceGui (stuck on a part's face). It gives all of them three settings: Enabled (show or hide everything), ResetOnSpawn (rebuild the UI when the player respawns?) and ZIndexBehavior (how layering works). You never make a LayerCollector yourself.
kid.analogy: A LayerCollector is like a picture frame. The frame itself can be on your wall (ScreenGui), on a sign post that always turns to face you (BillboardGui), or glued onto a box (SurfaceGui). Whatever you put in the frame is your UI.
whenToUse: Turning a whole menu on or off at once (Enabled)
Keeping UI from resetting when the player dies (ResetOnSpawn)
Changing how ZIndex layering works for all the UI inside (ZIndexBehavior)
kid.where: It is a base class, so you use ScreenGui, BillboardGui or SurfaceGui instead. Those usually live in StarterGui (copied into each player's PlayerGui). Control them from a LocalScript.

terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on the player's own device. UI code goes in LocalScripts, because each player has their own copy of the UI.
terms.client: The player's own device: their computer, phone, tablet or console.
terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the game for everyone at once.
terms.StarterGui: A folder in Explorer. UI you put here is copied to every player when they spawn.
terms.PlayerGui: Each player's own personal UI folder (inside their Player object). Only UI in here actually shows on their screen.
terms.descendant: Anything inside an object: children, grandchildren, and so on.
terms.base class: A 'parent type' other types are built from. You can't create it directly, but its properties appear on every type built from it.
terms.respawn: When your character comes back to life after dying or resetting.
terms.ZIndex: A layer number on each UI object. Higher numbers are drawn on top.
terms.sibling: Objects that share the same parent, like brothers and sisters.
terms.deprecated: Old and replaced by something better. Don't use it in new code.

examples.title: Keep a score display from resetting when you die
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local scoreGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
scoreGui.Name = "ScoreGui"
scoreGui.ResetOnSpawn = false -- keep this UI when the character respawns
scoreGui.Parent = playerGui

local label = Instance.new("TextLabel")
label.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 50)
label.Text = "Score: 0"
label.Parent = scoreGui

task.wait(5)
scoreGui.Enabled = false -- hide the whole thing at once
explain: We make a ScreenGui (a kind of LayerCollector) and put it straight into this player's PlayerGui.
ResetOnSpawn = false means it won't be deleted and rebuilt every time the character respawns.
After 5 seconds, Enabled = false hides the whole ScreenGui and everything inside it in one step.

gotchas: ResetOnSpawn is true by default. If your UI 'forgets' things after the player dies, this is usually why.
ResetOnSpawn = false only works if the Gui is DIRECTLY inside StarterGui, not inside a Folder in StarterGui.
With Enabled = false, nothing inside is drawn or clickable, and it stops updating.

class/Lighting.d:
The Lighting service controls global lighting in an experience. It includes a range of adjustable properties that you can use to change how lighting appears and interacts with other objects, as summarized in Lighting Properties.

Lighting may also contain an Atmosphere object to render realistic atmospheric effects, including particle density, haze, glare, and color. See Atmospheric Effects for details.

In addition, Lighting (along with Workspace.CurrentCamera) may contain post‑processing effects such as SunRaysEffect and BlurEffect.
class/Lighting.s: The `Lighting` service controls global lighting in an experience. It includes a range of adjustable properties that you can use to change how lighting appears and interacts with other objects.

m.d:
Ambient is the lighting hue applied to areas that are occluded from the sky, such as indoor areas.

Ambient defaults to [0, 0, 0] (black). As long as the red, green, and blue channels of this property do not exceed the corresponding channels in OutdoorAmbient, the change in hue will be reserved for areas occluded from the sun/moon.

Note that when GlobalShadows is disabled, there is no distinction between areas occluded from the sky and non‑occluded areas. In this case, OutdoorAmbient will be ignored and the hue from the Ambient property will be applied everywhere.
m.s: The lighting hue applied to areas that are occluded from the sky, such as indoor areas.

kid.simple: The color of light in places the sun cannot reach, like indoors or under a roof. Default is black (0, 0, 0). Brighter colors make those shadowy places lighter.
kid.example:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")
Lighting.Ambient = Color3.fromRGB(70, 70, 70) -- lighter indoor areas

m.d:
The intensity of illumination in the place.

Changing this value will influence the impact of the light source (sun or moon) on the place's lighting. Note that Ambient and OutdoorAmbient can also be used to influence how bright a place appears. For example, setting OutdoorAmbient to [255, 255, 255] will make the place appear brighter than its default value of 127, 127, 127 (as it is more white).
m.s: The intensity of illumination in the place.

kid.simple: How strong the sun or moon light is. Higher numbers make sunlit areas brighter.

m.d:
A numerical representation (in hours) of the current time of day used by Lighting. Note that this property does not correspond with the actual time of day and will not change during gameplay unless it has been changed by a script.

For a measure of Lighting time formatted as a 24-hour string, use TimeOfDay. Changing TimeOfDay or using SetMinutesAfterMidnight() will also change this property.
m.s: A numerical representation (in hours) of the current time of day used by `Lighting`.

kid.simple: The time of day as a number of hours, from 0 to 24. 6 is sunrise-ish, 12 is noon, 18 is evening, 0 is midnight. It only changes if a script changes it.

m.d:
The hue represented in light reflected in the opposite surfaces to those facing the sun or moon.

The surfaces of a BasePart influenced by ColorShift_Bottom depends on the position and orientation of the BasePart relative to the sun or moon's position. Where the sun is directly overhead a BasePart, the shift in color will only apply to the bottom surface.

This effect can be increased or reduced by altering Brightness.

Note that ColorShift_Top and ColorShift_Bottom will interact with the Ambient and OutdoorAmbient properties if they are greater than [0, 0, 0]. Also note that the influence of ColorShift_Bottom can be very hard to identify when GlobalShadows is enabled (default).
m.s: The hue represented in light reflected in the opposite surfaces to those facing the sun or moon.

kid.simple: A color tint added to the sides of parts facing AWAY from the sun or moon.
kid.example:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")
Lighting.ColorShift_Bottom = Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 80) -- bluish undersides

m.d:
The hue represented in light reflected from surfaces facing the sun or moon.

The surfaces of a BasePart influenced by ColorShift_Top depends on the position and orientation of the BasePart relative to the sun or moon's position. Where the sun is directly overhead a BasePart, the shift in color will only apply to the top surface.

This effect can be increased or reduced by altering Brightness.

Note that ColorShift_Top and ColorShift_Bottom will interact with the Ambient and OutdoorAmbient properties if they are greater than [0, 0, 0].
m.s: The hue represented in light reflected from surfaces facing the sun or moon.

kid.simple: A color tint added to the sides of parts facing TOWARD the sun or moon. Orange looks like a warm sunset.
kid.example:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")
Lighting.ColorShift_Top = Color3.fromRGB(255, 150, 50) -- warm sunlight

m.d: Ambient light that is derived from the environment with a default of 0. This property is similar to Ambient and OutdoorAmbient but it's dynamic and can change according to the sky and time of day. When this property is increased, it's recommended to decrease Ambient and OutdoorAmbient accordingly.
m.s: Ambient light that is derived from the environment.

kid.simple: How much soft light comes from the sky itself, from 0 to 1. Unlike Ambient, it changes with the sky and the time of day.

m.d: Specular light derived from environment with a default of 0. This property will make smooth objects reflect the environment and it is especially important to make metal look more realistic.
m.s: Specular light derived from environment.

kid.simple: How much smooth and metal surfaces reflect the sky around them, from 0 to 1. Makes metal look more real.

m.d: This property determines the exposure compensation amount which applies a bias to the exposure level of the scene prior to the tonemap step. Defaults to 0 (no exposure compensation) and has a range from -5 to 5. A value of 1 indicates twice as much exposure and -1 means half as much exposure.
m.s: The exposure compensation value.

kid.simple: Brightens or darkens the whole picture, from -5 to 5. 1 is twice as bright, -1 is half as bright, 0 is normal.
kid.example:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")
Lighting.ExposureCompensation = -1 -- a darker scene

m.d:
Unused. The maximum Range of PointLight, SpotLight, and SurfaceLight objects is always 120 studs; this property does not change that clamp.

This property is typed as RolloutState. It is non-scriptable and hidden in the Studio Properties window.
m.s: Unused. Light `Class.PointLight.Range|Range` is always clamped to 120 studs.

kid.simple: Unused hidden setting. Lights are always limited to a range of 120 studs anyway.

m.d: A Color3 value giving the hue of Lighting fog. Note that fog properties are hidden when Lighting contains an Atmosphere object.
m.s: A `Datatype.Color3` value giving the hue of `Lighting` fog.

kid.simple: The color of the fog.

m.d: The depth from the Workspace.CurrentCamera, in studs, at which fog will be completely opaque. Note that fog properties are hidden when Lighting contains an Atmosphere object.
m.s: The depth from the `Class.Workspace.CurrentCamera`, in studs, at which fog will be completely opaque.

kid.simple: How far from the camera, in studs, the fog becomes completely solid. Smaller numbers mean thicker fog.

m.d: The depth from the Workspace.CurrentCamera, in studs, at which fog begins to show. Note that fog properties are hidden when Lighting contains an Atmosphere object.
m.s: The depth from the `Class.Workspace.CurrentCamera`, in studs, at which fog begins to show.

kid.simple: How far from the camera, in studs, the fog starts to appear.

m.d:
The geographic latitude, in degrees, of the scene, influencing the result of Lighting time on the position of the sun and moon. When calculating the position of the sun, the earth's tilt is also taken into account.

Changing GeographicLatitude will alter the position of the sun at every TimeOfDay. If you're looking to obtain the sun or moon's position, use GetSunDirection() or GetMoonDirection().
m.s: The geographic latitude, in degrees, of the scene, influencing the result of `Lighting` time on the position of the sun and moon.

kid.simple: Pretends your world is at a place on Earth this many degrees north or south. It changes the sun's path across the sky at each time of day.
kid.example:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")
Lighting.GeographicLatitude = 60 -- far north: lower sun

m.d:
Toggles voxel-based dynamic lighting in the place. When set to true, shadows are rendered in sheltered areas depending on the position of the sun and moon. The lighting hue applied to these sheltered areas is determined by the Ambient property while the lighting hue in all other areas is determined by the OutdoorAmbient property.

When false, shadows are not drawn and no distinction is made between indoor and outdoor areas. As a result, the Ambient property determines the lighting hue and OutdoorAmbient will do nothing.

Shadows are calculated using a voxel system and each lighting voxel is 4×4×4 studs. This means objects need to be larger than 4×4×4 studs to display a realistic shadow. Shadows are also recalculated when BaseParts are moving.
m.s: Toggles voxel-based dynamic lighting for the place.

kid.simple: If true, the sun and moon cast shadows, and sheltered areas get the darker Ambient color.

m.d: LightingStyle indicates the artistic intent behind lighting in the experience, as an LightingStyle option. LightingStyle.Soft is the stylized look; LightingStyle.Realistic is the naturalistic look. The actual shadowing path also depends on PrioritizeLightingQuality (for example, Soft with that property enabled uses shadow maps rather than voxel lighting).
m.s: The artistic intent behind lighting in the experience.

kid.simple: The overall art style of the light: Soft (more cartoony) or Realistic (more like real life).

m.d:
OutdoorAmbient is the lighting hue applied to outdoor areas.

OutdoorAmbient defaults to [127, 127, 127]. As long as the red, green, and blue channels of Ambient do not exceed the corresponding channels in OutdoorAmbient, the hue of the lighting in outdoor areas will be determined by this property.

The effective OutdoorAmbient value is clamped to be greater than or equal to Ambient in all channels, meaning that if a channel of Ambient exceeds its corresponding OutdoorAmbient channel, the hue of Ambient will begin to apply to outdoor areas.

Note that when GlobalShadows is disabled, there is no distinction between areas occluded from the sky and non‑occluded areas. In this case, OutdoorAmbient will be ignored and the hue from the Ambient property will be applied everywhere.
m.s: The lighting hue applied to outdoor areas.

kid.simple: The color of soft fill light outdoors. Default is gray (127, 127, 127). Whiter makes outside look brighter.

m.d:
This property determines whether outlines are enabled or disabled in a place.

Outlines can be disabled on a global basis, using this Lighting property, or alternatively on a surface-by-surface basis for BaseParts using SurfaceType.

Although this property can be set by scripts, it recommended this property is set in Roblox Studio prior to publishing the place.
m.s: Determines whether outlines are enabled or disabled in a place.
m.dep: This item is no longer supported as the outlines feature was removed from the Roblox platform.

kid.simple: Old — outlines on parts are no longer drawn.

m.d: This property indicates whether you prefer lighting/shading quality or view distance to scale down first. As the rendering quality level reduces, a setting of true prioritizes features such as advanced shadows and high‑quality shaders at closer distances, while a setting of false prioritizes view distance.
m.s: Indicates whether you prefer lighting/shading quality or view distance to scale down first.

kid.simple: On slower devices, decides what to lower first: if true, keep nice lighting and shadows up close and draw less far away; if false, keep the view distance and simplify lighting.

m.d: This is supposed to change the color of player shadows, but currently doesn't do anything.
m.s: This is supposed to change the color of player shadows, but currently doesn't do anything.
m.dep: This item is deprecated and has no current functionality. Do not use it for new work.

kid.simple: Old — no longer used. Use `Ambient` to change shadow color.

m.d: Controls how blurry the shadows are with a default of 0.2. This property only works when Technology mode is ShadowMap or Future and the device is capable of rendering shadow maps.
m.s: Controls how blurry the shadows are.

kid.simple: How blurry shadow edges are, from 0 (sharp) to 1 (very soft). Default 0.2. Only works with the newer lighting modes on devices that support them.

m.d: Determines the lighting system for rendering the 3D world. This property is non‑scriptable and only modifiable in Studio.
m.s: Determines the lighting system for rendering the 3D world. Non-scriptable.
m.dep: This property has been superseded by LightingStyle which determines the artistic intent behind lighting, and PrioritizeLightingQuality which indicates whether you prefer lighting/shading quality or view distance to scale down first.

kid.simple: Old — set the lighting mode in Studio, and use `LightingStyle` and `PrioritizeLightingQuality` instead.

m.d:
A 24-hour string representation of the current time of day used by Lighting. For example:

local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")

Lighting.TimeOfDay = "11:00" -- Set time of day to 11:00 AM
Lighting.TimeOfDay = "21:30" -- Set time of day to 9:30 PM

Note that this property does not correspond with the real-world time of day and will not change during gameplay unless it has been changed by a script.

For a numeric measure of Lighting time, use ClockTime. Changing ClockTime or using SetMinutesAfterMidnight() will also change this property.
m.s: A 24-hour string representation of the current time of day used by `Lighting`.

kid.simple: The time of day as text on a 24-hour clock, like "14:00:00" for 2 PM or "21:30:00" for 9:30 PM. Changing it also changes ClockTime.

m.d:
Returns the number of minutes that have passed after midnight for the purposes of lighting. This number will be nearly identical to ClockTime multiplied by 60.

Note that this number will not always be equal to the value given in SetMinutesAfterMidnight() as it returns minutes after midnight in the current day.
m.s: Returns the number of minutes that have passed after midnight for the purposes of lighting.

kid.simple: Gives how many minutes past midnight the lighting clock is. About ClockTime times 60, so 2 PM gives 840.

m.dep: This method is a deprecated variant of Lighting:GetMinutesAfterMidnight() which should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use `GetMinutesAfterMidnight` instead.

m.d:
Returns a Vector3 representing the direction of the moon from the position (0, 0, 0). Note that when the moon has "set" and is no longer visible, the Vector3 returned by this method will continue to point towards the moon below the horizon.

GetSunDirection() is a variant of this method for obtaining the direction of the sun.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector3` representing the direction of the moon.

r.s: Vector3 representing the direction of the moon.

kid.simple: Gives a direction (a Vector3 of length 1) pointing from the center of the world toward the moon. It still points at the moon even when the moon is below the horizon.

m.d: Returns the moon's current phase. There is no way to change the moon's phase so this will always return 0.75.
m.s: Returns the moon's current phase.
m.dep: There is currently no way to change the moon's phase, and thus this method should not be used.

kid.simple: Old — no longer used.

m.d:
Returns a Vector3 representing the direction of the sun from the position (0, 0, 0). Note that when the sun has "set" and is no longer visible, the Vector3 returned by this method will continue to point towards the sun below the horizon.

GetMoonDirection() is a variant of this method for obtaining the direction of the moon.
m.s: Returns a `Datatype.Vector3` representing the direction of the sun.

r.s: Vector3 representing the direction of the sun.

kid.simple: Gives a direction (a Vector3 of length 1) pointing from the center of the world toward the sun. If its Y is below 0, the sun has set.
kid.example:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")
if Lighting:GetSunDirection().Y < 0 then
	print("It is night")
end

m.d:
Sets TimeOfDay and ClockTime to the given number of minutes after midnight.

This method allows a numerical value to be used, for example in a day/night cycle Script, without the need to convert to a string in the format required by TimeOfDay. It also allows values greater than 24 hours to be given that correspond to times in the next day.

The following code sample includes a simple day/night cycle script. The speed of time and the initial time can be changed using the TIME_SPEED and START_TIME parameters.
m.s: Sets `Class.Lighting.TimeOfDay|TimeOfDay` and `Class.Lighting.ClockTime|ClockTime` to the given number of minutes after midnight.

p.s: The number of minutes after midnight.

kid.simple: Sets the time of day using minutes after midnight, so you can use plain numbers. 720 is noon, 1080 is 6 PM.

m.dep: This method is a deprecated variant of Lighting:SetMinutesAfterMidnight() which should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use `SetMinutesAfterMidnight` instead.

m.d:
This event fires when a Lighting property is changed or a Sky is added or removed from Lighting. See the skyChanged parameter for when that flag is true versus false. Some Lighting property changes never fire this event:

  • Changing GlobalShadows will not fire this event.
  • Changing fog properties FogColor, FogStart, or FogEnd will not fire this event.

In cases where this behavior is not desired, the Object.Changed event or Object:GetPropertyChangedSignal() method can be used.
m.s: This event fires when a `Lighting` property is changed or a `Class.Sky` is added or removed from `Lighting`.

p.s: true when a Sky is added or removed, or when a Sky property other than Sky.SkyboxOrientation changes. false for Lighting property changes, Atmosphere property changes, and SkyboxOrientation changes.

kid.simple: Fires when a Lighting setting changes or a Sky is added or removed. It gives true if the change was about the sky.
kid.example:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")
Lighting.LightingChanged:Connect(function(skyChanged)
	print("Lighting changed. Sky changed?", skyChanged)
end)
kid.gotcha: It does not fire for fog or GlobalShadows changes. Use `GetPropertyChangedSignal` for those.

kid.simple: Lighting controls the look of the whole world's light: the time of day, how bright the sun is, the color of shadows, and fog. You can also put a Sky, an Atmosphere, and effects like Bloom or Blur inside it. Changing Lighting can make your game feel sunny, spooky, or like a sunset.
kid.analogy: Lighting is like the light switches, dimmer, and window blinds for your whole world. Turn the clock to night and the sun goes down; add fog and the far-away things fade into mist.
whenToUse: Make a day and night cycle by changing the time.
Set the mood: dark and foggy for horror, bright and colorful for an obby.
Hold Sky, Atmosphere, and post-processing effects like BloomEffect or ColorCorrectionEffect.
kid.where: A service on both server and client. Get it with `game:GetService("Lighting")`. Changes made by a server Script are seen by everyone; changes made in a LocalScript are seen only by that player.

terms.service: A special built-in object at the top of the game. Get one with `game:GetService("Name")`.
terms.Color3: A color made of red, green, and blue amounts. `Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)` is red.
terms.ambient light: Soft light that fills everything, even places the sun cannot reach directly. It decides how dark shadows are.
terms.fog: A haze that makes far-away things fade into a color.
terms.exposure: How bright the whole picture is made, like a camera letting in more or less light.
terms.specular: Shiny highlights and reflections on smooth surfaces.
terms.latitude: How far north or south on Earth a place is. It changes the sun's path in the sky.
terms.post-processing effect: A filter applied to the whole picture after it is drawn, like blur or extra glow.
terms.deprecated: Old and replaced by something newer.

examples.title: Day and night cycle
examples.code:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")

-- One full day takes 4 minutes (240 seconds)
local secondsPerDay = 240

while true do
	-- ClockTime goes from 0 to 24 (hours). Move it forward a little each step.
	Lighting.ClockTime = (Lighting.ClockTime + 24 / secondsPerDay * 0.1) % 24
	task.wait(0.1)
end
explain: ClockTime is the hour of the day, from 0 (midnight) to 24. 14 means 2 PM.
Every 0.1 seconds we add a tiny bit of time. 24 hours spread over 240 seconds is 0.1 hours per second.
`% 24` wraps it back to 0 after midnight, so the cycle repeats forever.

examples.title: Spooky fog
examples.code:
local Lighting = game:GetService("Lighting")

Lighting.ClockTime = 0                          -- midnight
Lighting.FogColor = Color3.fromRGB(40, 40, 50)  -- dark gray-blue
Lighting.FogStart = 0                           -- fog starts right at the camera
Lighting.FogEnd = 80                            -- fully foggy 80 studs away
explain: The time is set to midnight.
Fog begins at 0 studs from the camera and becomes completely solid at 80 studs, so you can barely see far.
If Lighting has an Atmosphere inside, these fog settings are hidden; use the Atmosphere instead.

gotchas: Fog settings stop working when an Atmosphere object is inside Lighting. Use the Atmosphere's Density and Haze instead.
Time does not move on its own. You need a script (like the day/night example) to change it.
Changes from a LocalScript only show for that player, which is useful for things like a personal night-vision effect.

class/LineForce.d:
The LineForce constraint applies a force along the theoretical line connecting its two Attachments. As the end points (attachments) move, the direction of force will change accordingly.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Force Location

By default, force is applied to either parent at its attachment location. If desired, force can be focused at each parent's center of mass by enabling ApplyAtCenterOfMass.

Inverse Square Law

When InverseSquareLaw is true, the force magnitude is multiplied by the inverse square of the distance, meaning the force will increase exponentially as the two attachments get closer together, like magnets. When using this setting, it's recommended that you set a MaxForce threshold to prevent infinite force if the attachments align precisely.

Reactionary Force

By default, the constraint only applies force to Attachment0, while Attachment1 remains unaffected. However, force can be applied to both attachments in equal and opposite directions by enabling ReactionForceEnabled.
class/LineForce.s: Applies a force along the theoretical line connecting its two `Class.Attachment|Attachments`.

m.d: When true, force is applied at the center of mass of the parent assembly of Attachment0, and the line determining the direction of the force will start at the said center of mass. When false, force is applied at Attachment0 and the line determining the direction will also start at Attachment0.
m.s: Whether force is applied at the center of mass of the parent assembly.

kid.simple: If true, the force pushes through the balance point of Attachment0's part (no spinning), and the line starts there. If false, it pushes at Attachment0 itself.

m.d: When true, the force magnitude is multiplied by the inverse square of the distance.
m.s: When `true`, the force magnitude is multiplied by the inverse square of the distance.

kid.simple: If true, the force gets much stronger as the two attachments get closer: at half the distance it is 4 times stronger. Great for magnets.
kid.example:
local pull = workspace.Ball.LineForce
pull.InverseSquareLaw = true
pull.MaxForce = 5000 -- always add a cap with this on
kid.gotcha: Set MaxForce too, or parts can explode apart when they almost touch.

m.d: The magnitude of the force.
m.s: The magnitude of the force.

kid.simple: How strong the push or pull is. Positive pulls Attachment0 toward Attachment1; negative pushes it away.
kid.example:
local push = workspace.Ball.LineForce
push.Magnitude = -3000 -- push the ball AWAY from the target

m.d: The maximum absolute force that can be applied. This property is enabled only when InverseSquareLaw is also enabled. This property is mainly used to address the issue that the force of the body mover becomes infinite the closer the two attachments are, causing explosions that can't be prevented by scripts. This property bounds the force's absolute value.
m.s: Maximum absolute force that can be applied.

kid.simple: The most force allowed. Only used when InverseSquareLaw is true, to stop the force getting endlessly big when the attachments are very close.

m.d: Enables a reaction force (equal an opposite) to be applied to the parent of Attachment1. By default line force only applies a force on the parent of Attachment0 and uses Attachment1 as the target direction without any dynamic relationship.
m.s: Enables an equal and opposite reaction force on the parent of `Class.Constraint.Attachment1|Attachment1`.

kid.simple: If true, the Attachment1 part gets pushed too, the same amount in the opposite direction, so both parts pull toward (or push away from) each other. If false (default), only Attachment0's part moves.
kid.example:
-- Two unanchored balls that attract each other
workspace.BallA.LineForce.ReactionForceEnabled = true

kid.simple: LineForce pushes or pulls a part along the straight line between two attachments. As the attachments move, the direction of the push follows them. A positive Magnitude pulls Attachment0 toward Attachment1, like a tractor beam; a negative one pushes it away.
kid.analogy: LineForce is like an invisible magnet string between two points. Wherever the target goes, the pull points straight at it.
whenToUse: Tractor beams or homing pulls toward a point
Pushing things away from an explosion center or force field
kid.where: Create with Instance.new("LineForce") in a Script, set Attachment0 (the part that gets pushed) and Attachment1 (the target), and put it in workspace.

terms.force: A push or pull. In Roblox it is measured in Roblox force units (mass x studs per second per second). A bigger number is a harder push.
terms.mass: How much 'stuff' an object has, which decides how hard it is to push. A part's mass = its volume x its material density. A 4x1x2 Plastic part (volume 8, density 0.7) has mass 5.6.
terms.gravity: The pull that makes things fall. In Roblox it is `workspace.Gravity`, which is 196.2 studs per second per second by default.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.center of mass: The balance point of an object. Pushing exactly through it moves the object without spinning it; pushing off to the side also makes it spin.
terms.magnitude: The length (size) of a vector, ignoring its direction. The magnitude of Vector3.new(3, 4, 0) is 5.
terms.MaxForce: A cap (upper limit) on how hard a constraint is allowed to push. It is a limit, not the amount it always pushes.
terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.inverse square law: A rule where force gets much stronger as things get closer: half the distance means 4 times the force, a third of the distance means 9 times. Real magnets and gravity work roughly like this.
terms.reaction force: The 'push back'. If you push a wall, the wall pushes you back just as hard. With a reaction force, both parts get pulled toward each other.

examples.title: Magnet that pulls a ball toward it
examples.code:
local magnet = workspace:WaitForChild("Magnet") -- anchored part
local ball = workspace:WaitForChild("Ball")     -- unanchored part

local target = Instance.new("Attachment")
target.Parent = magnet
local pulled = Instance.new("Attachment")
pulled.Parent = ball

local pull = Instance.new("LineForce")
pull.Attachment0 = pulled   -- this part gets pulled
pull.Attachment1 = target   -- toward this point
pull.Magnitude = 2000       -- positive = pull closer
pull.InverseSquareLaw = true -- stronger when closer, like a real magnet
pull.MaxForce = 5000        -- never push harder than this
pull.ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true
pull.Parent = ball
explain: Attachment0 is in the ball, so the ball is what moves. Attachment1 in the magnet is the target.
Magnitude 2000 is the strength. A positive number pulls the ball toward the magnet.
InverseSquareLaw makes the pull grow fast as the ball gets close.
MaxForce stops the pull from becoming gigantic when the ball is almost touching the magnet, which could make it fly off.

gotchas: With InverseSquareLaw on and no MaxForce, the force can become huge when the attachments get very close and fling parts away. Always set MaxForce.
MaxForce only does anything when InverseSquareLaw is true.
By default only the Attachment0 part is pushed. Turn on ReactionForceEnabled if both parts should feel it.
Remember gravity: to lift a part, Magnitude must beat its weight (mass x 196.2).

class/LinearVelocity.d:
The LinearVelocity constraint applies force on an assembly to maintain a constant linear velocity. It can be set to apply force along a Vector3, line, or 2D plane. Alternatively:

  • If you want to control the amount of force applied, use a VectorForce constraint.
  • If you only need initial linear velocity, set the AssemblyLinearVelocity property directly on the assembly.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Relativity

Application of velocity can be controlled through the constraint's RelativeTo property. If set to World, force will be applied in world coordinates, independent of the parent or attachment orientations. If set to Attachment0 or Attachment1, force will be applied relative to Attachment0 or Attachment1 respectively.
class/LinearVelocity.s: Applies force on an assembly to maintain a constant linear velocity.

m.d: Determines how the constraint force will be limited. When set to Magnitude, the constraint force will have a magnitude less than MaxForce. When set to PerAxis, the force along each axis will be less than the corresponding value in MaxAxesForce when VelocityConstraintMode is Vector or the corresponding value in MaxPlanarAxesForce when VelocityConstraintMode is Plane. Only used when ForceLimitsEnabled is true.
m.s: Determines how the constraint force will be limited.

kid.simple: How the force is limited (only when ForceLimitsEnabled is true). Magnitude: total push is capped by MaxForce. PerAxis: each direction gets its own cap from MaxAxesForce or MaxPlanarAxesForce.
kid.example:
local mover = workspace.Platform.LinearVelocity
mover.ForceLimitMode = Enum.ForceLimitMode.PerAxis
mover.MaxAxesForce = Vector3.new(5000, 100000, 5000) -- strong up/down, gentle sideways

m.d: Determines if the constraint force will be limited or if the physics solver can apply an unlimited force to achieve the target velocity. When enabled, the constraint force is limited based on ForceLimitMode. When disabled, the physics solver will always apply a force that is large enough to achieve the target velocity.
m.s: Determines if the constraint force will be limited or if the physics solver can apply an unlimited force to achieve the target velocity.

kid.simple: If true, the force is capped by the limit settings. If false, the physics engine uses as much force as it takes to hit the target speed exactly.

m.d: The normalized Vector3 direction for constraining the velocity along a line, when VelocityConstraintMode is set to Line.
m.s: The normalized `Datatype.Vector3` direction for constraining the velocity along a line.

kid.simple: In Line mode, the direction (a length-1 Vector3) that the speed is measured along.
kid.example:
local mover = workspace.Platform.LinearVelocity
mover.VelocityConstraintMode = Enum.VelocityConstraintMode.Line
mover.LineDirection = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0) -- up and down, like an elevator

m.d: Float value of the velocity when VelocityConstraintMode is set to Line.
m.s: Float value of the velocity when `Class.LinearVelocity.VelocityConstraintMode|VelocityConstraintMode` is set to `Enum.VelocityConstraintMode|Line`.

kid.simple: In Line mode, the target speed along LineDirection in studs per second. Negative goes the opposite way.
kid.example:
local mover = workspace.Platform.LinearVelocity
mover.LineVelocity = 5   -- go up at 5 studs/s
task.wait(4)
mover.LineVelocity = -5  -- now come back down

m.d: Maximum force along each axis that the constraint can apply to achieve the target velocity. Only used if ForceLimitsEnabled is true, ForceLimitMode is PerAxis, and VelocityConstraintMode is Vector. The axes used to apply the limit correspond to the RelativeTo property.
m.s: Maximum force along each axis that the constraint can apply to achieve the vector velocity. Only used if `Class.LinearVelocity.ForceLimitsEnabled|ForceLimitsEnabled` is `true`, `Class.LinearVelocity.ForceLimitMode|ForceLimitMode` is `Enum.ForceLimitMode|PerAxis`, and `Class.LinearVelocity.VelocityConstraintMode|VelocityConstraintMode` is `Enum.VelocityConstraintMode|Vector`.

kid.simple: In Vector mode with PerAxis limits on, the most force allowed in each of X, Y and Z separately.
kid.example:
local mover = workspace.Platform.LinearVelocity
mover.ForceLimitMode = Enum.ForceLimitMode.PerAxis
mover.MaxAxesForce = Vector3.new(1000, 20000, 1000)

m.d: Maximum magnitude of the force vector the constraint can apply. Only used if ForceLimitsEnabled is true and ForceLimitMode is Magnitude.
m.s: Maximum magnitude of the force vector the constraint can apply.

kid.simple: The most total force the constraint may use to reach the target speed (when limits are on and ForceLimitMode is Magnitude). It is a cap, not the amount it always pushes.
kid.gotcha: Too small and the part may never reach the speed, or may sag under gravity.

m.d: Maximum force along each axis that the constraint can apply to achieve the plane velocity. Only used if ForceLimitsEnabled is true, ForceLimitMode is PerAxis, and VelocityConstraintMode is Plane. The axes used to apply the limit correspond to the RelativeTo property.
m.s: Maximum force along each axis that the constraint can apply to achieve the plane velocity. Only used if `Class.LinearVelocity.ForceLimitsEnabled|ForceLimitsEnabled` is `true`, `Class.LinearVelocity.ForceLimitMode|ForceLimitMode` is `Enum.ForceLimitMode|PerAxis`, and `Class.LinearVelocity.VelocityConstraintMode|VelocityConstraintMode` is `Enum.VelocityConstraintMode|Plane`.

kid.simple: In Plane mode with PerAxis limits on, the most force allowed along each of the two directions of the flat surface, as a Vector2.
kid.example:
local mover = workspace.Puck.LinearVelocity
mover.ForceLimitMode = Enum.ForceLimitMode.PerAxis
mover.MaxPlanarAxesForce = Vector2.new(3000, 3000)

m.d: Vector2 value of the velocity in each tangent direction of the plane, when VelocityConstraintMode is set to Plane.
m.s: `Datatype.Vector2` value of the velocity in each tangent direction of the plane.

kid.simple: In Plane mode, the target speed across a flat surface as a Vector2: the first number is along PrimaryTangentAxis, the second along SecondaryTangentAxis. Movement off the surface (like falling) is left free.
kid.example:
local mover = workspace.Puck.LinearVelocity
mover.VelocityConstraintMode = Enum.VelocityConstraintMode.Plane
mover.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
mover.PrimaryTangentAxis = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0)
mover.SecondaryTangentAxis = Vector3.new(0, 0, 1)
mover.PlaneVelocity = Vector2.new(10, 5) -- 10 along X, 5 along Z, gravity still works

m.d:
The primary axis in the plane, when VelocityConstraintMode is set to Plane. Value depends on the value of RelativeTo as follows:

  • If RelativeTo is set to Attachment0, this axis is the Axis of Attachment0.
  • If RelativeTo is set to Attachment1, this axis is the Axis of Attachment1.
  • If RelativeTo is set to World, this value must be specified in the world space.
m.s: The primary axis in the plane, when `Class.LinearVelocity.VelocityConstraintMode|VelocityConstraintMode` is set to `Enum.VelocityConstraintMode|Plane`.

kid.simple: In Plane mode, the first direction across the flat surface. With RelativeTo = World you type it in world directions; with Attachment0 or Attachment1 it is that attachment's main (X) arrow.

m.d:
Determines whether the constraint applies an equal and opposite reaction force to the assembly of Attachment1. Defaults to true. This reaction force is relevant when RelativeTo is ActuatorRelativeTo.Attachment1 — the mode in which the constraint drives the Attachment0 assembly's velocity relative to the Attachment1 assembly. Because RelativeTo defaults to ActuatorRelativeTo.World, this property is typically only meaningful once RelativeTo is set to Attachment1.

When enabled in that mode, the constraint applies the reaction force to the Attachment1 assembly, coupling the two assemblies. When disabled, the constraint applies force only to the Attachment0 assembly; the Attachment1 assembly receives no reaction force, though its pose and velocity are still read as the reference frame for the target velocity.
m.s: Determines whether an equal and opposite reaction force is also applied to the assembly of `Class.Constraint.Attachment1|Attachment1` when `Class.LinearVelocity.RelativeTo|RelativeTo` is `Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo|Attachment1`.

kid.simple: Matters when RelativeTo is Attachment1. If true (default), the Attachment1 part gets pushed back the opposite way too, so the two are linked. If false, only the Attachment0 part is pushed.
kid.example:
local mover = workspace.Car.LinearVelocity
mover.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.Attachment1
mover.ReactionForceEnabled = false -- do not push the other part back

m.d: Sets the ActuatorRelativeTo property for the constraint.
m.s: Sets the `Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo` property for the constraint.

kid.simple: Picks whose directions the velocity uses: World (fixed game directions), Attachment0 (turns with the moving part) or Attachment1 (speed is measured compared to the other attachment's part).
kid.example:
local mover = workspace.Boat.LinearVelocity
mover.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.Attachment0
mover.VectorVelocity = Vector3.new(0, 0, -15) -- forward along the boat's own front, wherever it faces

m.d:
The secondary axis in the plane, when VelocityConstraintMode is set to Plane. Value depends on the value of RelativeTo as follows:

  • If RelativeTo is set to Attachment0, this axis is the SecondaryAxis of Attachment0.
  • If RelativeTo is set to Attachment1, this axis is the SecondaryAxis of Attachment1.
  • If RelativeTo is set to World, this value must be specified in the world space.
m.s: The secondary axis in the plane, when `Class.LinearVelocity.VelocityConstraintMode|VelocityConstraintMode` is set to `Enum.VelocityConstraintMode|Plane`.

kid.simple: In Plane mode, the second direction across the flat surface. With RelativeTo = World you type it in world directions; with an attachment it is that attachment's secondary (Y) arrow.

m.d: Vector3 velocity value when VelocityConstraintMode is set to Vector.
m.s: `Datatype.Vector3` velocity value when `Class.LinearVelocity.VelocityConstraintMode|VelocityConstraintMode` is set to `Enum.VelocityConstraintMode|Vector`.

kid.simple: In Vector mode (the default), the target speed in all three directions as a Vector3, in studs per second.

m.d: The mode of the constraint: Line, Plane, or Vector. Default is Vector.
m.s: The mode of the constraint.

kid.simple: Picks what to control: Vector (default, all three directions), Line (one direction only) or Plane (two directions across a flat surface).

LinearVelocity makes a part move at a steady speed that you choose. Instead of pushing a fixed amount like VectorForce, it pushes just enough (up to a limit) to keep the part at exactly that speed. It can control speed in all directions, along one line, or across a flat surface.
kid.analogy: LinearVelocity is like cruise control in a car. You pick 20 studs per second, and it presses the gas harder going uphill and softer going downhill to stay at 20.
whenToUse: Moving platforms or elevators that travel at a steady speed
Conveyor belts that carry things along
Projectiles that fly straight at a fixed speed
Dashes and knockbacks that last a moment
kid.where: Create with Instance.new("LinearVelocity"), set Attachment0 to an attachment in the part to move, and put it in workspace. Usually from a Script on the server.

terms.velocity: Speed plus direction, written as a Vector3 in studs per second. Vector3.new(0, 0, 20) means 20 studs every second along the Z direction.
terms.force: A push or pull. In Roblox it is measured in Roblox force units (mass x studs per second per second). A bigger number is a harder push.
terms.mass: How much 'stuff' an object has, which decides how hard it is to push. A part's mass = its volume x its material density. A 4x1x2 Plastic part (volume 8, density 0.7) has mass 5.6.
terms.gravity: The pull that makes things fall. In Roblox it is `workspace.Gravity`, which is 196.2 studs per second per second by default.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) bundled together. Used for positions, directions, forces and speeds. Y is up.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.assembly: A group of parts that are rigidly joined (for example by welds) so they move as one solid object. A force on any part moves the whole group.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.world space: Directions measured using the whole game world's fixed arrows: Y is always straight up toward the sky, no matter how a part is turned.
terms.attachment space: Directions measured using an attachment's own arrows. If the part tips over, 'up' for the attachment tips over too.
terms.RelativeTo: Chooses whose arrows the numbers use: World (the game world's fixed directions) or Attachment0/Attachment1 (that attachment's own directions, which turn when the part turns).
terms.MaxForce: A cap (upper limit) on how hard a constraint is allowed to push. It is a limit, not the amount it always pushes.
terms.magnitude: The length (size) of a vector, ignoring its direction. The magnitude of Vector3.new(3, 4, 0) is 5.
terms.axis: An imaginary line something turns around or slides along. An attachment's X axis is its main arrow.
terms.Vector2: Two numbers (X, Y) bundled together. Used here for a speed across a flat surface: one number for each of the two directions on that surface.
terms.normalized / unit vector: A direction arrow whose length is exactly 1. Vector3.new(1, 0, 0) is a unit vector pointing along X. Use `.Unit` on any Vector3 to get one.
terms.VelocityConstraintMode: Picks what to control: Vector (speed in all 3 directions), Line (speed along just one line) or Plane (speed across a flat surface, leaving the up/down free).
terms.force limit: The most force the constraint may use. If the limit is too small, the part may never reach the target speed (for example if it cannot beat gravity).

examples.title: A part that flies forward at 20 studs per second
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 2)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Anchored = false
part.Parent = workspace

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

local mover = Instance.new("LinearVelocity")
mover.Attachment0 = attachment
mover.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
mover.VelocityConstraintMode = Enum.VelocityConstraintMode.Vector
mover.VectorVelocity = Vector3.new(0, 0, 20) -- 20 studs every second along Z
mover.MaxForce = math.huge                   -- allowed to push as hard as needed
mover.Parent = part
explain: VectorVelocity (0, 0, 20) is the goal speed: 20 studs per second in the +Z direction, 0 up/down, 0 sideways.
Because the Y speed is 0, the constraint also fights gravity to keep the part from falling.
math.huge means 'no real limit', so it can always push hard enough. A small MaxForce might lose to gravity (a 5.6-mass part needs about 1098.7 just to stay up).

examples.title: Slide along a line but let gravity work
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 2)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Anchored = false
part.Parent = workspace

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

local slide = Instance.new("LinearVelocity")
slide.Attachment0 = attachment
slide.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
slide.VelocityConstraintMode = Enum.VelocityConstraintMode.Line
slide.LineDirection = Vector3.new(1, 0, 0) -- only control movement along X
slide.LineVelocity = 10                     -- 10 studs per second along X
slide.MaxForce = 10000
slide.Parent = part
explain: In Line mode, only speed along LineDirection is controlled. Here that is the X direction.
The part moves 10 studs per second along X but can still fall or move freely in Y and Z, so gravity still pulls it down.

gotchas: If the part does not move, MaxForce may be too low. Remember gravity alone needs mass x 196.2. Try math.huge to test.
In Vector mode with Y = 0, the part will not fall, because 0 up/down speed is part of the goal.
With RelativeTo = Attachment0, the direction turns with the part. Use World if you want a fixed direction.

class/LocalScript.d:
A LocalScript is a Luau source container that runs its contents on the client (player's device) instead of the server. It is used to access client-only objects such as the player's Camera.

For code run through LocalScripts, the LocalPlayer property of the Players service will return the player whose client is running the script.

See here for a table of valid container services from which LocalScripts will execute.
class/LocalScript.s: An object that contains and runs Luau code on the client (player's device) instead of the server.

kid.simple: A LocalScript holds Luau code that runs on one player's own device (the client), not on the server. It controls things only that player has: their camera, their screen buttons, their keyboard and mouse. Changes a LocalScript makes to the world are usually seen only by that one player.
kid.analogy: If the server is the referee, each client is one player on the field with their own eyes and hands. A LocalScript is like that player's personal notebook: it can change what THEY see and do, but it cannot change the score for everyone.
whenToUse: Reacting to keyboard, mouse, touch, or controller input.
Making buttons and menus on the screen work.
Moving or changing the player's camera.
Visual effects only one player should see, like a sparkle when they pick something up.
kid.where: Runs on the client. A LocalScript only runs when it is inside one of these: StarterPlayerScripts (copied into each player's PlayerScripts), StarterCharacterScripts (copied into the character each time it spawns), StarterGui (copied into the PlayerGui), StarterPack (copied into the Backpack), ReplicatedFirst, or the player's character. It does NOT run in Workspace (outside a character), ReplicatedStorage, ServerScriptService, or ServerStorage. Use `Players.LocalPlayer` to get the player it is running for.

terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the one shared copy of the game for everyone in the server. What happens here is the truth everyone sees.
terms.client: One player's own device (computer, phone, tablet, or console). Each player has their own client.
terms.LocalPlayer: `game:GetService("Players").LocalPlayer` is the player whose device is running this LocalScript. It only works in LocalScripts.
terms.StarterPlayerScripts: A folder inside StarterPlayer. LocalScripts here start once when the player joins.
terms.StarterCharacterScripts: A folder inside StarterPlayer. LocalScripts here are copied into the character every time it spawns.
terms.StarterGui: The folder for screen menus (ScreenGuis). Its contents are copied to each player's screen.
terms.RemoteEvent: A messenger object that lets a LocalScript send a message to a server Script, or the other way around.
terms.replicate: To copy changes between the server and players' devices. Most changes made by a LocalScript are NOT copied to the server.

examples.title: Press E to print a message
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")

local player = Players.LocalPlayer -- the player using this device

UserInputService.InputBegan:Connect(function(input, gameProcessed)
	-- gameProcessed is true if they were typing in chat, so ignore that
	if gameProcessed then return end
	if input.KeyCode == Enum.KeyCode.E then
		print(player.Name, "pressed E")
	end
end)
explain: Keyboard input only exists on the player's device, so this must be a LocalScript.
`Players.LocalPlayer` is you, the player whose computer is running this.
When E is pressed (and they are not typing in chat), it prints a message in that player's Output.

examples.title: Ask the server to do something
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts (plus a RemoteEvent named BuyItem in ReplicatedStorage)
examples.code:
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local buyItem = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("BuyItem") -- a RemoteEvent

-- Tell the server we want to buy a sword.
-- A Script on the server listens with buyItem.OnServerEvent and decides if it is allowed.
buyItem:FireServer("Sword")
explain: LocalScripts cannot give items for real, because the server is in charge.
So the LocalScript sends a request through a RemoteEvent.
A server Script receives it, checks if the player has enough coins, and then gives the item.

gotchas: A LocalScript in Workspace (not inside a character) or in ReplicatedStorage simply never runs. Put it in StarterPlayerScripts, StarterCharacterScripts, or StarterGui.
Use `WaitForChild` to find things, because objects from the server may arrive a moment after your LocalScript starts.
Changes made only in a LocalScript (like deleting a wall) are NOT seen by other players. Use a RemoteEvent to ask the server.
LocalScripts cannot see ServerStorage or ServerScriptService; those stay on the server.

Returns an Array, where each element of the returned Array is itself an Array of entries in the same format as described in LocalizationTable:GetEntries(). The order of the elements in the returned Array is the same order that the LocalizationTables will be searched through to attempt automated localization for the provided Instance. The entry elements within a particular LocalizationTable are returned in an unspecified order.

This function returns entries regardless of whether the object is a GuiBase2d with GuiBase2d.AutoLocalize enabled. An object that is a GuiBase2d will not actually be automatically localized unless GuiBase2d.AutoLocalize is enabled.

The ordering of the tables is as follows:

  • First, it looks for the earliest GuiBase2d ancestor of the object (including the provided object) that has a GuiBase2d.RootLocalizationTable. Tables then append in the same order as described in GuiBase2d.RootLocalizationTable by going up through the LocalizationTable ancestors of that GuiBase2d.RootLocalizationTable. If no such GuiBase2d.RootLocalizationTable is found, no tables append in this step. If instance is nil, no tables append in this step.
  • Next, tables from the LocalizationTable hierarchy under LocalizationService append. For each child LocalizationTable of LocalizationService, it appends tables going up from the lowest descendant LocalizationTable of the tables parented to the service, all the way up to the children of the service. If there are no children of LocalizationService that are LocalizationTables, then no tables append in this step.
  • Finally, the cloud LocalizationTable appends to the array. If there is no cloud LocalizationTable, or the cloud LocalizationTable has not yet loaded, then no table appends in this step.

This function does not yield. It will not wait until the cloud LocalizationTable has loaded.

class/LocalizationTable.d:
A LocalizationTable is a database of translations. It contains source strings and translations for various languages. It is used with the Translator and LocalizationService auto-translator system to control text translations in the game. LocalizationTables are designed to be treated as resources, like a texture or a script. They are not optimized to be modified at runtime. Changing the contents of a table will cause the entire contents of the table to be replicated to all players.

LocalizationTable Entries

Each LocalizationTable contains a set of entries. Each entry contains the translations of the text, along with some special fields:

  • Key is an optional unique key for fast hash lookups in code. If it is non-empty it must be unique in the table.
  • Source is the original text in the source language that will be used by the LocalizationService automatic text replacement system to match GUI text and render a translation instead. The Source field can be filled by the text capture tools, or can be set manually. For key-based lookups the Source value can be used as a translation for LocalizationTable.SourceLocaleId if the entry doesn't have a translation for that locale. If Source is empty then the entry will not be used by the automatic replacement system.
  • Context is the full Instance name for the object that the text appeared on. Context is used for disambiguation by the automatic text replacement system. When multiple matches for the Source are found, the system will pick the best match by matching backwards from the end of the Context string. There are other more robust ways to handle disambiguation available as well, like using multiple tables with GuiBase2d.RootLocalizationTable.
  • Example is whatever you want it to be. If the text capture tool guessed some parameters for a string the Example field will contain an example of them used in context.

All of these fields are optional, but at least either Key or Source must be non-empty. No two entries can have the same Key, Source, and Context.

See Translating Dynamic Content for more information.

class/LogService.d:
LogService allows you to log structured log entries and read outputted text. For logging scoped to a named, hierarchical path, use LogService:GetLogger() to obtain a Logger.

Template Syntax

Methods that accept a context table support {key} template placeholders in the message string. To include a literal brace character in the output, use double braces: {{ produces a literal { and }} produces a literal }.

local LogService = game:GetService("LogService")

LogService:Info("Value = {{result}}: {val}", {val = 42})
-- Output: "Value = {result}: 42"

Context Values

The context table accepts any value type. Non-serializable values are automatically converted to strings in the stored context:

  • Instances are stored as their full path (e.g., "Workspace.MyModel.Part")
  • Functions are stored as "<function>"
  • Other non-primitive types are stored using their tostring() representation

Mixed tables (tables with both string and numeric keys) and pure arrays are accepted. Numeric keys are converted to string keys (e.g., index 1 becomes key "1"). If a numeric key collides with an existing string key, the explicit string key takes precedence.

local LogService = game:GetService("LogService")

-- Instance values are converted to their full path
LogService:Info("Touched {part}", {part = workspace.MyPart})
-- Context stores: {part = "Workspace.MyPart"}

-- Mixed tables are accepted; numeric keys become string keys
LogService:Info("Player {name}", {name = "Alice", 1, 2, 3})
-- Context stores: {name = "Alice", ["1"] = 1, ["2"] = 2, ["3"] = 3}

Warning

This service might have unexpected or unreliable behavior and content might be truncated. Don't rely on contents of events and messages emitted by this service for any important game logic.

Logs a message at the MessageType.MessageError level and throws a structured error with optional context. As this method always throws, use LuaGlobals.pcall() to catch the error. The thrown error is a table with message, template, context, and stack fields, and a __tostring metamethod that returns the rendered message.

When a context table is provided, template placeholders like {key} in the message are replaced with the corresponding context values.

local LogService = game:GetService("LogService")

local ok, err = pcall(function()
    LogService:Error("Failed: {reason}", {reason = "timeout"})
end)
-- ok is false
-- err.message == "Failed: timeout"
-- err.context == {reason = "timeout"}
-- tostring(err) == "Failed: timeout"

Returns a table of tables, each with the message string, message type, and timestamp of a message that the client displays in the Output window. Each inner table contains the following keys:

  • message (string) -- the rendered message text.
  • messageType (MessageType) -- the log level (MessageOutput, MessageInfo, MessageWarning, or MessageError).
  • timestamp (number) -- the time the message was emitted, in seconds.
  • context (dictionary) -- the structured key-value pairs if the message was emitted via a structured logging method; absent otherwise.

The history is capped at a maximum of 512 entries by default. Calling LogService:ClearOutput() empties the history, so subsequent calls return only entries logged after the clear.

class/Logger.d:
A Logger emits structured log entries that are tagged with a hierarchical name, letting you group related messages by subsystem or feature. Obtain a top-level logger from LogService:GetLogger(), then create nested child loggers with Logger:GetLogger(). Each logger has a short Logger.Name and a dot-joined Logger.FullPath built from its ancestry (for example a logger named Damage created from a logger named Combat has the full path Combat.Damage).

local LogService = game:GetService("LogService")

local combat = LogService:GetLogger("Combat")
local damage = combat:GetLogger("Damage")

print(damage.Name)      --> Damage
print(damage.FullPath)  --> Combat.Damage

damage:Info("Dealt {amount} damage to {target}", {amount = 25, target = "Goblin"})

Loggers behave the same as the structured logging methods on LogService: messages flow to the Output window, the Developer Console, and LogService.MessageOut, and are included in LogService:GetLogHistory() tagged with the logger's full path.

Hierarchy and Propagation

When a message is logged on a logger, its Logger.MessageOut event fires on that logger and on every ancestor up to the root. This lets you attach a listener on a parent logger to observe all messages emitted by its descendants. The message is emitted to the engine's output system exactly once, tagged with the originating logger's full path.

Template Syntax and Context

The logging methods accept the same {key} template placeholders and context tables as the structured logging methods on LogService. See LogService for details on template syntax and how context values are stored.

Lifetime

A logger remains valid as long as you hold a reference to it. Once all references to a logger (and its descendants) are released, it is reclaimed, and calling any method on a stale logger raises an error. The number of live loggers and the length of a logger's full path are both bounded; exceeding either limit raises an error from Logger:GetLogger().

Warning

This class might have unexpected or unreliable behavior and content might be truncated. Don't rely on contents of events and messages emitted by loggers for any important game logic.
